cards.q: What is Rapid PVST+?
cards.a: Rapid PVST+ (Rapid Per-VLAN Spanning Tree Plus) is Cisco's implementation of RSTP (IEEE 802.1w) running as a separate spanning-tree instance for each VLAN, combining RSTP rapid-convergence mechanics with per-VLAN PVST+ architecture.

cards.q: Why is it incorrect to confuse Rapid PVST+ with classic PVST+?
cards.a: Rapid PVST+ is RSTP per VLAN, while classic PVST+ is based on 802.1D STP per VLAN.

cards.q: How does Rapid PVST+ achieve per-VLAN load balancing?
cards.a: Each VLAN has its own RSTP instance and can elect a different Root Bridge, so different VLANs prefer different paths and both redundant uplinks carry useful traffic. Load balancing is achieved by intentionally placing different VLAN roots on different switches.

cards.q: Does Rapid PVST+ automatically load-balance traffic?
cards.a: No. Rapid PVST+ does not automatically load-balance; you must intentionally place different VLAN roots on different switches to distribute load.

cards.q: What are the Rapid PVST+ operational port states?
cards.a: Discarding, Learning, and Forwarding (not the classic Blocking/Listening/Learning/Forwarding).

cards.q: What are the Rapid PVST+ port roles?
cards.a: Root, Designated, Alternate, and Backup, evaluated per Rapid PVST+ instance rather than per physical interface.

cards.q: How do you compute the effective Bridge ID priority in Rapid PVST+?
cards.a: Effective priority = configured priority + VLAN ID (e.g., 4096 + VLAN 10 = 4106). The Extended System ID puts the 12-bit VLAN ID in the Bridge ID, and configurable priorities are in increments of 4096 (default 32768).

cards.q: How does Proposal/Agreement work in Rapid PVST+?
cards.a: SW1 sends a Proposal toward SW2; SW2 synchronizes its relevant ports and replies with Agreement, allowing SW1 to rapidly transition its port to Forwarding without the long classic timer sequence, while keeping the topology synchronized.

cards.q: Why should you not memorize that Rapid PVST+ converges in 1-3 seconds or 6 seconds?
cards.a: 1-3 seconds is not a fixed protocol timer, and 6 seconds (3 missed BPDUs × 2 s) is only a failure-detection rule of thumb. Actual convergence depends on failure type, topology, alternate-path availability, link type, device behavior, and configuration.

cards.q: What is the default Rapid PVST+ Hello interval and the missed-BPDU failure detection rule?
cards.a: Default Hello is 2 seconds. RSTP can consider a neighbor lost after approximately three missed BPDUs, giving roughly 6 seconds as a failure-detection rule of thumb (distinct from convergence time).

cards.q: What is an edge port/PortFast used for in Rapid PVST+, and why should it not be used on switch-to-switch links?
cards.a: PortFast/edge ports connect to end devices (PC, server, printer, IP phone) and move rapidly to Forwarding. It should not be used as a replacement for STP on switch-to-switch links.

cards.q: How does BPDU Guard protect a Rapid PVST+ edge port, and does PortFast disable STP?
cards.a: BPDU Guard protects an edge port by error-disabling it if an unexpected BPDU arrives. PortFast does not disable STP; BPDU Guard provides the protection against unexpected BPDUs.

cards.q: What command configures VLAN-specific path cost and VLAN-specific port priority?
cards.a: interface G0/1 then spanning-tree vlan 10 cost 4 sets per-VLAN cost; spanning-tree vlan 10 port-priority 64 sets per-VLAN port priority (default 128, in increments of 16).

cards.q: What happens when Rapid PVST+ interoperates with a classic 802.1D STP neighbor?
cards.a: RSTP must interoperate with the slower protocol on that connection/instance, so the legacy boundary can behave with slower 802.1D behavior, reducing rapid-convergence benefits.

cards.q: How does Rapid PVST+ interoperate with MST?
cards.a: At an MST boundary the MST region participates through its Common and Internal Spanning Tree (CIST). MST maps VLANs into fewer instances, so it is not simply one tree for all VLANs.

cards.q: How do Rapid PVST+ and MST compare regarding VLAN handling and scaling?
cards.a: Rapid PVST+ runs one instance per VLAN (per-VLAN control, more CPU/memory as VLANs grow); MST maps multiple VLANs to fewer instances (more scalable). For many VLANs, MST is often considered.

cards.q: What is the main operational trade-off of Rapid PVST+?
cards.a: It combines per-VLAN control, rapid convergence, and easy Cisco operation, but at the cost of more STP instances and more CPU/memory/BPDU processing.

cards.q: What command enables Rapid PVST+ and what command sets a VLAN root?
cards.a: spanning-tree mode rapid-pvst enables it; spanning-tree vlan 10 priority 4096 or spanning-tree vlan 10 root primary sets/designates a root. root secondary makes a predictable backup (commonly resulting in 28672 under default conditions).

cards.q: Which commands verify Rapid PVST+ mode, a specific VLAN, and inconsistent ports?
cards.a: show spanning-tree summary confirms mode and features; show spanning-tree vlan 10 views a VLAN; show spanning-tree root views roots; show spanning-tree inconsistentports views inconsistent ports; show spanning-tree active views active instances.

cards.q: What is the logical load-balancing design using two distribution switches?
cards.a: Configure VLAN 10 root on DIST1 and VLAN 20 root on DIST2 so Uplink A carries VLAN 10 traffic and Uplink B carries VLAN 20 traffic. This is STP-level load distribution, not a single VLAN forwarding over both redundant paths simultaneously.

cards.q: A physical interface can have different STP roles for different VLANs. Give an example.
cards.a: Gi0/1 can be a Root Port for VLAN 10, a Designated Port for VLAN 20, and an Alternate Port for VLAN 30, because STP role is evaluated per Rapid PVST+ instance.

cards.q: Why does more VLANs mean more Rapid PVST+ instances, and what is the consequence?
cards.a: Each VLAN runs its own RSTP instance (1 VLAN = 1 instance, 100 VLANs = potentially 100 instances), increasing CPU/memory/BPDU load, which is one reason MST can scale better.

cards.q: Why is MST not one tree for all VLANs?
cards.a: MST maps VLANs into MST instances, and multiple MST instances can have different topologies, so it is not simply a single spanning tree for everything.

cards.q: What is the final memory rule for the STP implementation family?
cards.a: PVST+ = 802.1D per VLAN; Rapid PVST+ = 802.1w per VLAN; MST = RSTP-style multiple instances with VLANs mapped into instances.

cards.q: What are the key Rapid PVST+ facts in quick review?
cards.a: Foundation RSTP/IEEE 802.1w; one RSTP instance per VLAN; Root per VLAN; states Discarding/Learning/Forwarding; roles Root/Designated/Alternate/Backup; rapid mechanism Proposal/Agreement; default Hello 2 s; edge feature PortFast; protection BPDU Guard; missed-BPDU rule of thumb 6 s; command spanning-tree mode rapid-pvst.
